svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra cross-tenant access settings and trust. Cross-tenant access has three dials: outbound access settings in the user's home tenant controlling whether their users can reach external organizations, inbound access settings in the resource tenant controlling whether external users can reach its resources, and inbound trust settings determining whether the resource tenant's Conditional Access policies trust multifactor authentication, compliant device and Microsoft Entra hybrid joined device claims from the external organization. The defaults are that B2B collaboration is enabled for all external organizations, B2B direct connect is blocked entirely in both directions, and MFA and device claims from other organizations are not trusted. Organizational settings take precedence over default settings and there is no limit on the number of organizations. In the authentication flow, the security token service evaluates the resource tenant's Conditional Access policies and checks the home tenant's outbound settings together with the resource tenant's inbound settings, then checks inbound trust settings, then looks in the user's authentication session for an MFA or device claim; if the requirement is not met a challenge is issued in the home tenant. With no trust configured, B2B collaboration users are challenged for MFA in the resource tenant while B2B direct connect users are blocked outright, and if device compliance cannot be evaluated both are blocked. The authentication strength method table shows that SMS as second factor, voice call, Microsoft Authenticator push notification and OATH software token are acceptable in both the home tenant and the resource tenant, while Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in, OATH hardware token, FIDO2 security key, Windows Hello for Business and certificate-based authentication are acceptable in the home tenant only. Therefore refusing to trust the partner's MFA makes phishing-resistant authentication strength unachievable for external users. Risk-based policies have limits: user risk is evaluated in the home directory and cannot be resolved in the resource tenant, a required password change blocks the external user, the risky users report does not reflect external users, and admins cannot dismiss or remediate them. Devices can only be managed by a user's home tenant. Trusting MFA also conflicts with the ID Protection MFA registration policy, where having both present means external users cannot satisfy the requirements for access. Configuring trust settings requires a Microsoft Entra ID P1 licence on the configuring tenant, and B2B direct connect requires P1 in both tenants plus mutual configuration. Changes to cross-tenant access settings are protected actions and are audited under the CrossTenantAccessSettings category.
svg.title: Trust is not a relaxation: it decides where a check happens, and only one place can perform the strong ones
svg.text: Refusing to trust a partner’s MFA does not move the check to you at full strength.
It moves it to you at reduced strength — or, for B2B direct connect, blocks the user outright.
Three dials, and the defaults are not uniform
Outbound (home tenant)
can my users reach the other organisation?
B2B collab: ON by default
Inbound (resource tenant)
can their users reach my resources?
Direct connect: BLOCKED
Trust (inbound only)
do I accept their MFA and device claims?
NOT trusted by default
Every sign-in consults both tenants: “Fabrikam’s outbound settings and Contoso’s inbound settings”. No limit on organisations,
and organisational settings take precedence over defaults. Trusting MFA is not waving people through: a missing claim means
“Microsoft Entra ID issues MFA and device challenges in the user’s home tenant as needed.”
Table 1 is the whole argument: where a method counts
AUTHENTICATION METHOD
HOME TENANT
RESOURCE TENANT
SMS · voice call · Authenticator push · OATH software token
accepted
accepted
Authenticator phone sign-in · OATH hardware token
accepted
NOT accepted
FIDO2 security key
accepted
NOT accepted
Windows Hello for Business
accepted
NOT accepted
Certificate-based authentication
accepted
NOT accepted
Every phishing-resistant method is home-tenant-only. So a phishing-resistant strength policy WITH trust disabled requires
something the user has no way to perform. The secure posture is: trust the claim, then raise the bar.
With no trust configured, and MFA required
B2B collaboration user — challenged, must “satisfy MFA in
the resource tenant”, using only the weaker method set
B2B direct connect user — BLOCKED. Not challenged.
You “must configure your inbound trust settings”.
Device compliance required but not evaluable — both
blocked. “Devices can only be managed by a user’s home
tenant”, so without device trust it is a block, not a control.
Approved client app and app protection: never available.
The deadlock that neither screen shows you
“Consider excluding external users from the… ID Protection
MFA registration policy, if you’re going to trust MFA for
external users. When both policies are present, external
users aren’t able to satisfy the requirements for access.”
One policy says enrol MFA here; the other says their home
MFA counts. The user can neither enrol nor proceed, and
nothing about either setting looks wrong on its own page.
Same shape as post #41a: policies compose, silently.
Risk-based policy does not survive the tenant boundary
User risk
evaluated in their HOME directory — “can’t be resolved in the resource tenant”
Sign-in risk
evaluated in YOUR directory, in real time
Require password change on high risk
blocks them — they cannot reset a password in your directory
Your risky users report
does not list them, and you cannot dismiss or remediate them
Sign-in risk policy requiring MFA
blocks unregistered users on purpose — stops an attacker enrolling their own
Before tightening anything: every external organisation is enabled by default and nobody has an inventory, while the sign-in
logs you would discover it from are “only retained for 30 days”. Trust settings need P1; direct connect needs P1 in BOTH tenants.
Changes here are protected actions, audited under CrossTenantAccessSettings — a log worth alerting on, not just keeping.
Sources: Cross-tenant access overview, and Authentication and Conditional Access for B2B users, on Microsoft Learn.
